pages.wrong_reason: Mis-attributed hypothesis: CG24 contains no LWE-based construction. Per the paper's abstract (eprint 2024/235, verified), pseudorandomness of all its codes rests on LPN-type assumptions — either 2^{O(sqrt(n))}-hardness of LPN, or polynomial hardness of LPN together with the planted XOR assumption at low density. The zero-bit PRC is the LDPC-based construction (Section 5.1 of CG24) and, under those assumptions, tolerates every constant substitution rate p < 1/2. The hypothesis should be an LPN-type assumption, not LWE; the sibling page subexponential-lpn-to-prc-cg24 already records the correct attribution for the L-bit case. The parameter claim in the migrated bullet (codeword length O(secpar^2/log secpar), robustness eps < 1/2 - 1/poly) rides on the same mis-attributed construction and must be re-verified against CG24's LPN parameterization before being re-recorded on a corrected edge.
flags: The sibling edge lwe-to-prc-cg24 carries the same LWE-vs-LPN mis-attribution (its own Notes flag it); both originate from bullets on pseudorandom-error-correcting-code.md § Other results, which need fixing.
Correct replacement edge: {subexponential-lpn} => zero-bit-prc with source CG24 (or {lpn, planted-xor} => zero-bit-prc for the polynomial-hardness variant).

sources.ref_file_title: BM88 - Arthur-merlin games A randomized proof system and a hierarchy of complexity classes
sources.note: Journal version of Babai's STOC 1985 paper 'Trading group theory for randomness', which introduced the MA/AM hierarchy; BM88 is the wiki's existing page and the standard citation for MA ⊆ AM.

pages.class_justification: Proven unconditional containment between complexity classes; by repo convention (cf. bpp-to-am-gs86, qcma-to-qma) such inclusions carry class free.
pages.statement: $\classMA \subseteq \classAM$: every language with a [[merlin-arthur|Merlin–Arthur]] proof system has an [[arthur-merlin|Arthur–Merlin]] proof system — [[BM88 - Arthur-merlin games A randomized proof system and a hierarchy of complexity classes|BM88]].
pages.sketch: Amplify the MA verifier's soundness error below $2^{-(\ell+1)}$ by parallel repetition, where $\ell$ bounds the length of Merlin's message, then reverse the message order: Arthur sends his coins first and Merlin answers. A union bound over all $2^{\ell}$ Merlin messages shows the swap costs at most a $2^{\ell}$ factor in soundness error, which the amplification absorbs.
flags: The migrated parenthetical justification ('Merlin's optimal strategy is independent of those coins') is not a correct proof, as the migration Notes already flag; the statement/sketch above replace it with the standard amplify-then-swap argument.
MA ⊆ AM is a theorem (Babai 1985 / Babai–Moran 1988), not folklore — frontmatter source: folklore should become the BM88 citation.

sources.ref_file_title: Ver92 - On the Power of PP
sources.note: Proc. 7th Annual Structure in Complexity Theory Conference, pp. 138–143. Proves MA ⊆ PP and gives an oracle relative to which AM ⊄ PP. Not in cryptobib; needs inline bibtex.

pages.class_justification: Proven unconditional containment between complexity classes; repo convention assigns class free to such inclusions.
pages.statement: $\classMA \subseteq \classPP$: every language with a [[merlin-arthur|Merlin–Arthur]] proof system is decidable in [[probabilistic-polynomial-time|probabilistic polynomial time]] with unbounded error — [[Ver92 - On the Power of PP|Ver92]].
pages.sketch: Amplify the MA verifier's error below $2^{-(\ell+2)}$, where $\ell$ bounds the witness length. The PP machine samples a uniformly random witness and runs the amplified verifier: for $x \in L$ the acceptance probability is at least $2^{-\ell}(1-2^{-(\ell+2)})$, while for $x \notin L$ it is at most $2^{-(\ell+2)}$; shifting the acceptance threshold between the two bounds decides $L$ in $\classPP$.
flags: Resolves the page's explicit 'TODO citation'. Ver92 also shows an oracle relative to which AM is not contained in PP, which may be worth a separate barrier page.

Ver92 needs a new reference page with inline bibtex (venue not covered by cryptobib): @InProceedings, Proc. 7th Annual Structure in Complexity Theory Conference, IEEE, 1992, pages 138-143, doi 10.1109/SCT.1992.215389.

pages.class_justification: Immediate containment between complexity classes (a probabilistic verifier is a special case of a quantum verifier); repo convention assigns class free to such inclusions.
pages.model_justification: Matches the repo convention for inclusions among quantum proof-system classes (cf. qcma-to-qma, qma-to-pp, bpp-to-bqp).
pages.statement: $\classMA \subseteq \classQCMA$: any [[merlin-arthur|Merlin–Arthur]] proof system is a [[quantum-classical-merlin-arthur|QCMA]] proof system — the witness is already classical, and a quantum verifier can run the classical probabilistic verification circuit with unchanged completeness and soundness — folklore.
pages.sketch: The quantum verifier evaluates the classical verification predicate as a quantum circuit, sampling the verifier's coins by measuring qubits prepared in the uniform superposition; acceptance probabilities are preserved exactly.
flags: Genuinely definitional, so folklore is the honest disposition; if a definitional citation is ever wanted, QCMA traces to Aharonov–Naveh, 'Quantum NP - A Survey' (arXiv:quant-ph/0210077).

sources.ref_file_title: BN00 - Authenticated Encryption Relations among Notions and Analysis of the Generic Composition Paradigm
sources.note: cryptobib_key: AC:BelNam00 (verified in vendor/cryptobib/crypto.bib, pp. 531–545). Journal version: J. Cryptology 21(4), 2008 (JC:BelNam08). Proves encrypt-then-MAC with a SUF-CMA MAC gives IND-CCA (via INT-CTXT + IND-CPA ⇒ IND-CCA), and that weak unforgeability does not suffice.

sources.ref_file_title: KY00 - Unforgeable Encryption and Chosen Ciphertext Secure Modes of Operation
sources.note: cryptobib_key: FSE:KatYun00 (verified in vendor/cryptobib/crypto.bib, pp. 284–299). Independent concurrent work: ciphertext unforgeability plus IND-CPA yields IND-CCA for symmetric encryption.

pages.class_justification: Encrypt-then-MAC is one fixed construction invoking the SKE scheme's $\Enc$/$\Dec$ and the MAC's $\Tag$/$\Vrfy$ only as oracles; the security reduction runs any IND-CCA adversary as an oracle, answering its decryption queries by rejecting every ciphertext-tag pair not produced by the encryption oracle (an accepted fresh pair is output as a MAC forgery). This is the standard RTV04 fully-black-box shape.
pages.statement: Let $\SKE$ be a [[symmetric-key-encryption#cpa-security|CPA-secure]] [[symmetric-key-encryption|SKE]] scheme and $\MAC$ a strongly unforgeable (SUF-CMA) [[message-authentication-code|MAC]]. The encrypt-then-MAC composition, which encrypts under an independent SKE key and tags the ciphertext under an independent MAC key, is a [[symmetric-key-encryption#cca-security|CCA-secure]] SKE scheme. Strong unforgeability is required: with a merely UF-CMA MAC the composition can fail to be CCA-secure — [[BN00 - Authenticated Encryption Relations among Notions and Analysis of the Generic Composition Paradigm|BN00]].
pages.sketch: Strong unforgeability of the MAC forces every decryption query on a pair $(c, t)$ not returned by the encryption oracle to decrypt to $\bot$ except with negligible probability, so the decryption oracle can be simulated by rejecting all fresh queries; CCA security of the composition then reduces to CPA security of $\SKE$.
pages.improvements_text: - Independently and concurrently, ciphertext unforgeability plus CPA security was shown to imply CCA security for symmetric encryption — [[KY00 - Unforgeable Encryption and Chosen Ciphertext Secure Modes of Operation|KY00]].
flags: Hypothesis 'ske' must be read as CPA-secure SKE and the MAC as strongly unforgeable; the wiki MAC page currently defines only UF-CMA, so the SUF-CMA qualifier lives in prose (a strong-unforgeability variant section on message-authentication-code.md would let it be linked).

The sibling migrated pages hash-function-to-ske and hash-function-to-mac carry the same OWF-chain bullet; the {CPA-SKE, MAC} => CCA-SKE link recorded here is the correct conjunctive final link of that composite chain.

Conclusion node cca-secure-symmetric-key-encryption resolves to the #cca-security variant anchor declared in symmetric-key-encryption.md frontmatter, so the edge does not collapse to SKE => SKE (contrary to one migration note).

pages.wrong_reason: False as stated under the standard simulation-based definitions: security against malicious adversaries does NOT imply security against (plain) semi-honest adversaries. The malicious-model simulator may substitute the corrupted party's input in the ideal execution, while the semi-honest simulator must reproduce the party's view on its actual input; there are protocols secure against malicious adversaries that are not secure against semi-honest ones. This is documented in Hazay–Lindell, 'A Note on the Relation between the Definitions of Security for Semi-Honest and Malicious Adversaries' (eprint 2010/551, verified) and in Goldreich's Foundations of Cryptography Vol. 2 (augmented semi-honest behavior, §7.4.4.1). The correct nearby edge is: malicious security implies AUGMENTED semi-honest security (semi-honest adversaries additionally allowed to substitute their input before the execution starts). Separately, neither endpoint (malicious-security, semi-honest-security) exists as a wiki object page — they are bullet definitions on interactive-protocol.md — so the edge has no addressable endpoints.
flags: If the corrected edge (malicious => augmented semi-honest) is wanted, source it to Goldreich Foundations Vol. 2 §7.4.4 and/or Hazay–Lindell eprint 2010/551, and first create object pages/anchors for the adversary models.
The source prose on interactive-protocol.md § Adversary models states the flat implication and should be corrected or caveated (skeptical-checker lane).

sources.note: cryptobib_key: EC:KilLyuSch18 (verified in vendor/cryptobib/crypto.bib, pp. 552–586). QROM treatment of Fiat–Shamir signatures; Dilithium-QROM variant under MLWE, MSIS, SelfTargetMSIS.

sources.ref_file_title: BBD+23 - Fixing and Mechanizing the Security Proof of Fiat-Shamir with Aborts and Dilithium
sources.authors: Manuel Barbosa, Gilles Barthe, Christian Doczkal, Jelle Don, Serge Fehr, Benjamin Grégoire, Yu-Hsuan Huang, Andreas Hülsing, Yi Lee, Xiaodi Wu
sources.note: cryptobib_key: C:BBDDFG23 (verified in vendor/cryptobib/crypto.bib, pp. 358–389). eprint 2023/246.

pages.class_justification: No source states an RTV-style class; the ROM proof rewinds the adversary via the forking lemma and is scoped to an idealized model, so recording a class would add a claim the sources do not make.
pages.model_justification: DKL+18 prove unforgeability in the (classical and quantum) random-oracle model — the challenge hash is modeled as a random oracle (Fiat–Shamir with aborts). Frontmatter currently says standard and must change to rom.
pages.statement: Dilithium (standardized as ML-DSA in FIPS 204) is a [[digital-signature|digital signature]] scheme obtained by applying Fiat–Shamir with aborts to a module-lattice identification scheme. In the random-oracle model it is strongly — in particular existentially — unforgeable under chosen-message attacks assuming hardness of [[learning-with-errors#module-lwe|Module LWE]] and [[shortest-integer-solution#module-sis|Module-SIS]] — [[DKL+18 - CRYSTALS-Dilithium A Lattice-Based Digital Signature Scheme|DKL+18]].
pages.sketch: The signer samples a short masking vector $\mathbf{y}$, commits to the high bits of $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y}$, derives the challenge $c$ by hashing commitment and message, and reveals $\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{y} + c\mathbf{s}_1$ only if rejection sampling passes, so signatures are independent of the secret. Module LWE makes the public key $(\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{t} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{s}_1 + \mathbf{s}_2)$ pseudorandom, and the forking lemma turns a forger into a short solution for $[\mathbf{A} \mid \mathbf{t}]$, i.e. a Module-SIS solution.
pages.security_loss: non-tight: classical-ROM reduction loses a forking-lemma factor over the adversary's random-oracle queries
pages.improvements_text:
- QROM security of Fiat–Shamir signatures, with a Dilithium variant proved secure under Module LWE, Module-SIS, and SelfTargetMSIS — [[KLS18 - A Concrete Treatment of Fiat-Shamir Signatures in the Quantum Random-Oracle Model|KLS18]].
- Gaps in the original Fiat–Shamir-with-aborts proofs (including Dilithium's) identified and repaired with machine-checked proofs — [[BBD+23 - Fixing and Mechanizing the Security Proof of Fiat-Shamir with Aborts and Dilithium|BBD+23]].
flags: model: standard must change to rom.

Resolves the migration note on the ambiguous 'Module LWE/SIS' slash: Dilithium's proof uses BOTH assumptions (conjunctive hyperedge is correct); shortest-integer-solution.md line 72, attributing Dilithium to Module-SIS alone, is wrong and should be fixed (skeptical-checker lane).
Conclusion node 'ds' is the generic digital-signature page; the EUF-CMA/SUF-CMA qualifier lives in the statement.

sources.ref_file_title: HHK17 - A Modular Analysis of the Fujisaki-Okamoto Transformation
sources.authors: Dennis Hofheinz, Kathrin Hövelmanns, Eike Kiltz
sources.note: cryptobib_key: TCC:HofHovKil17 (verified in vendor/cryptobib/crypto.bib, pp. 341–371). Companion rather than follow-up: the modular FO analysis (ROM and QROM) that Kyber's IND-CCA proof invokes.

pages.class_justification: No source states an RTV-style class; the IND-CCA proof goes through the Fujisaki–Okamoto transform in an idealized (random-oracle) model, which the RTV taxonomy does not classify.
pages.model_justification: The IND-CPA scheme is standard-model from Module LWE, but the IND-CCA KEM claim — the conclusion of this edge — is proved via an FO transform with implicit rejection in the random-oracle model (QROM bounds also given). Frontmatter currently says standard and must change to rom.
pages.statement: Kyber (standardized as ML-KEM in FIPS 203) is an IND-CCA-secure [[key-encapsulation-mechanism|KEM]] in the random-oracle model assuming hardness of [[learning-with-errors#module-lwe|Module LWE]] at module rank $k \in \{2,3,4\}$: an IND-CPA public-key encryption scheme built directly from Module LWE is converted into an IND-CCA KEM by a Fujisaki–Okamoto transform with implicit rejection — [[BDK+18 - CRYSTALS-Kyber A CCA-Secure Module-Lattice-Based KEM|BDK+18]].
pages.sketch: The CPA scheme is LPR-style over a module: the public key is $(\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{t} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{s} + \mathbf{e})$ and a ciphertext is a pair of compressed Module LWE samples encoding the message in the high-order bits, so key and ciphertext are pseudorandom under MLWE. The FO transform derives the encryption randomness and session key by hashing the message, and decapsulation re-encrypts to reject malformed ciphertexts, yielding IND-CCA in the ROM.
pages.improvements_text: - Kyber's IND-CCA proof instantiates the modular Fujisaki–Okamoto analysis, which gives the underlying ROM and QROM bounds — [[HHK17 - A Modular Analysis of the Fujisaki-Okamoto Transformation|HHK17]].
flags: model: standard must change to rom.

The second migrated quote (the LS15 editorial paragraph, including the incorrect 'k = n recovers plain LWE' claim) belongs to the LS15 reference page discussion, not to this edge, and should be dropped here; its error is handled on module-lwe-to-lwe-ls15.

sources.ref_file_title: LS15 - Worst-case to average-case reductions for module lattices
sources.note: Defines Module LWE and notes the rank-1 specialization to Ring LWE.

pages.class_justification: Both directions are the identity reduction: a rank-1 Module LWE instance is literally a Ring LWE instance and vice versa, so instances and adversaries are passed through unchanged — one fixed construction and one fixed reduction, each using its input only as an oracle.
pages.statement: [[learning-with-errors#module-lwe|Module LWE]] at module rank $k = 1$ is [[learning-with-errors#ring-lwe|Ring LWE]]: a rank-1 module over $R_q$ is $R_q$ itself, so the rank-1 MLWE distribution coincides with the RLWE distribution and the two problems are identical, with hardness transferring in both directions — [[LS15 - Worst-case to average-case reductions for module lattices|LS15]].
pages.sketch: A rank-1 MLWE sample $(\mathbf{a}, \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{s} \rangle + e)$ with $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{s} \in R_q$ is literally an RLWE sample $(a, a \cdot s + e)$; the identity map is a reduction in both directions.
flags: Definitional coincidence presumes matching conventions: LS15's M-LWE definition specializes at rank 1 to LPR10's R-LWE (same dual-ring and error-distribution setup).
Hypothesis node module-lwe-rank-1 resolves via the learning-with-errors frontmatter variant alias to #module-lwe; a dedicated anchor would make the rank-1 qualifier addressable.

The migrated LS15 editorial quote also contains the incorrect 'k = n recovers plain LWE' claim, handled as wrong_claim on module-lwe-to-lwe-ls15; only the k = 1 half is correct and it is the content of this page.

pages.wrong_reason: The claim 'Module LWE at rank k = n recovers plain LWE' (over a degree-n polynomial ring R_q) is false as stated: a rank-n module over a degree-n ring has total Z_q-dimension n^2, and the sample matrix is block-structured (negacyclic blocks), not uniform, so rank-n MLWE is neither syntactically nor known to be computationally equivalent to plain LWE in dimension n. Plain LWE is the specialization of MLWE at ring DEGREE 1 (R = Z) with arbitrary module rank n — that is the correct definitional edge, and the one LS15's interpolation actually supports (verified against LS15/eprint 2012/090 secondary descriptions: rank 1 recovers ring problems, degree 1 recovers unstructured problems). The source page learning-with-errors.md line 135 carries the same error — its parenthetical 'ring $R_q \cong \ZZ_q^n$' is a module isomorphism, not a ring isomorphism, and does not remove the multiplicative structure.
flags: Correct replacement edge: MLWE over R = Z (ring degree 1) at rank n <=> LWE, definitional, source LS15; the hypothesis node would need to be redefined (module-lwe-rank-n currently aliases to #module-lwe with the wrong reading).
learning-with-errors.md § Module LWE bullet 'When k = n: recovers plain LWE (fully unstructured, ring R_q ≅ Z_q^n)' needs the same fix (skeptical-checker lane).

Nontrivial (non-definitional) relations between MLWE and RLWE/LWE do exist — e.g. Albrecht–Deo, 'Large Modulus Ring-LWE ≥ Module-LWE' (ASIACRYPT 2017) — but they are different edges with different parameters, not this equivalence.
